cases.title: Twenty minutes instead of sixty
cases.situation: Pete, 41, lifting 3 years, general strength, full gym, 4 days a week, nothing hurts. Today is legs: squat 4 × 5 at 225, Romanian deadlift 3 × 8, leg press, leg curl, calf raise. He types: "I've got 20 minutes before we leave town. Skip it or do something?"
cases.today: The check-in offers 30, 45 or 60+ minutes. At 30 the app drops accessories from the end and cuts main lifts to 2 sets, never dropping a main lift. There is no 20-minute choice and the rules don't cover it.
cases.rec: Don't skip. Squat only gets warm-up sets, then 2 to 3 hard sets at the planned 225. If time is left, 2 sets of Romanian deadlift. Nothing else. It counts as a done session with no make-up work, and the weight can still go up next time if he earns it.
cases.why: A 2021 review on training when short on time says keep the big multi-joint lifts, warm up only for the lift itself, skip stretching, and that as few as 4 hard sets per muscle a week still make progress. A second review found strength holds on very little work when the weight stays heavy. Moderate evidence; no study of a single 20-minute session.

sources.t: No Time to Lift? Designing Time-Efficient Training Programs for Strength and Hypertrophy: A Narrative Review (Iversen, Norum, Schoenfeld, Fimland, Sports Medicine, 2021)

Maintaining physical performance: the minimal dose of exercise needed to preserve endurance and strength over time (Spiering, Mujika, Sharp, Foulis, Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research, 2021; abstract read)

cases.reply: Don't skip it. Warm up, then 2 or 3 hard sets of squats at 225, and 2 sets of RDLs if there's time. That counts as today's session, nothing to make up.
cases.short: Don’t skip. Warm up, then 2 to 3 hard squat sets at 225, and 2 sets of RDLs if there’s time. Counts as a done session.

cases.title: Shoulder is a 2 in the gym but wakes him at night
cases.situation: Dale, 46, lifting 5 years, strength, full gym. His right shoulder aches 2 out of 10 on bench (185 × 6) and settles in a few hours. He types: "It's fine in the gym, but it's been waking me up when I roll onto it for about two weeks."
cases.today: Discomfort at 3 out of 10 or below that settles within 24 hours is okay to train through, so nothing changes. The rules don't mention pain at night.
cases.rec: Add a rule: pain that keeps waking them at night, or has for a week or two, gets a doctor or physical therapist suggestion now, whatever the number in the gym. Meanwhile swap to a pressing variation that doesn't hurt and keep training. No guessing at what it is. This adds a safety rule; it loosens none.
cases.why: University of Iowa Health Care says to be seen when shoulder pain regularly disrupts sleep or isn't better after one to two weeks of home care. Cleveland Clinic lists night pain among the warning signs. Expert guidance, not trials. Fairly sure.

sources.t: Shoulder pain while sleeping: When it could be more than soreness (University of Iowa Health Care, 2026)
Shoulder Pain: 11 Common Conditions and Causes (Cleveland Clinic, 2022)

cases.reply: Dale, pain that wakes you up for two weeks is worth getting looked at by a doctor or a physical therapist, even if it's a 2 in the gym. Until then, swap bench for a press that doesn't hurt and keep training. Tell me what they say.
cases.short: Night pain for two weeks gets a doctor or physical therapist suggestion now, whatever the gym number. Swap to a pain-free press meanwhile.

cases.title: Stops at the bottom of the range and calls it a 5
cases.situation: Hannah, 25, lifting 8 months, wants muscle, full gym, nothing hurts. Dumbbell shoulder press, 25s, 3 sets of 8 to 12, meant to feel like a 7 to 8. Three sessions running she logs 8, 8, 8 and rates each set 5 out of 10. She types: "I hit my reps. Why isn't the weight going up?"
cases.today: Reps in the range but not at the top means same weight, chase reps. The easy rating changes nothing until every set reaches the top, and the coach doesn't raise it unless she asks.
cases.rec: The coach explains once: the range is something to climb, and the set ends when it feels like a 7 to 8, not at the first number. Same weight next time, go until it's actually hard. No increase on the rating alone. If she still stops at 8 after two reminders, ask what's holding her back.
cases.why: A 2021 analysis of how well lifters judge reps left found people have about one more rep than they think on average, with a bigger gap on higher-rep sets, and experience made no difference. So a "5" at 8 reps has plenty left. Moderate evidence (studies disagreed a lot with each other); the coaching steps are judgment. Same pattern as Hunter's Nov 22 answer on ratings that don't fit the reps.

sources.t: Accuracy in predicting repetitions to task failure in resistance exercise: A scoping review and exploratory meta-analysis (Halperin and others, Sports Medicine, 2021; read on the university record)

cases.reply: The 8 to 12 is a range to climb, not a finish line. Same 25s next time, and keep going until a set feels like a 7 or 8. Once you reach 12 on every set, the weight goes up.
cases.short: Explain the range once: same weight, keep going until a set is a real 7 to 8. No increase on the rating alone.

cases.title: Wants everything on bench for 8 weeks
cases.situation: Rob, 36, lifting 9 years, bench 285, wants 315 by spring, full gym, 4 days, nothing hurts. He types: "Bench three times a week for 8 weeks. What's the least I can do to keep my squat and deadlift?"
cases.today: A focus lift gets an extra set and faster jumps; on a one-lift program the other main lifts go to maintenance: 2 sets, weight held. The rules don't say how little is enough or for how long.
cases.rec: Yes, for one block of up to 8 weeks. Squat and deadlift once a week each, 2 sets, at the weights he lifts now: the weight stays, the sets drop. Then a normal block for legs before specializing again. At 60 and over, hold more: 2 to 3 sets, twice a week.
cases.why: A 2021 review of the least training needed to hold strength: younger lifters held strength and muscle for up to 32 weeks on one session a week and as little as one set per exercise, as long as the weight stayed heavy; older adults needed up to two sessions and 2 to 3 sets. Moderate evidence, not tested on advanced lifters. This confirms today's design.

sources.t: Maintaining physical performance: the minimal dose of exercise needed to preserve endurance and strength over time (Spiering, Mujika, Sharp, Foulis, Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research, 2021; abstract read)

cases.reply: Yes, for one 8-week block. Squat and deadlift once a week each, 2 sets at the weights you lift now; that's enough to hold them. After the block, legs get a normal block again.
cases.short: Yes, for one 8-week block: squat and deadlift once a week, 2 sets each, at today’s weights.

cases.title: Night-shift month: every check-in is red
cases.situation: Amy, 34, nurse, lifting 3 years, strength, full gym, nothing hurts, not ill. Three workouts in a row: about 5 hours of sleep, energy 30, red. She has 3 more weeks of night shifts.
cases.today: Each red day is a short session: main lifts at 2 sets, same weights, no increases. After three red days in a row the app starts a lighter week by itself: about half the sets and 10% lighter for 7 days. Hunter's Nov 23 answer (not in the rules yet) was to cut sets but keep pushing strength.
cases.rec: After 3 red check-ins in a row from sleep or stress, when the athlete says it will continue: no automatic lighter week and no 10% drop. Take one set off every exercise (never under 2 on main lifts), keep the weights, and allow half-size increases when every set hits the top at the target effort. Back to normal after two check-ins in a row that aren't red. This does not apply when the red comes from illness signs or soreness; those keep today's rules. Planned lighter weeks still happen.
cases.why: A 2018 systematic review found several short nights in a row lower force in big multi-joint lifts but not single-joint ones (abstract only; no numbers). A 2022 analysis put one bad night at about 3% off strength and about 10% off higher-rep work, and could not study runs of bad nights. Strength holds on fewer sets if the weight stays (Spiering, scenario 6). Nobody has tested this exact plan: coaching judgment.

sources.t: Inadequate sleep and muscle strength: implications for resistance training (Knowles and others, Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport, 2018; abstract read on the university record)
Effects of Acute Sleep Loss on Physical Performance: A Systematic and Meta-Analytical Review (Craven and others, Sports Medicine, 2022)
How much does sleep loss affect strength performance? (Greg Nuckols, Stronger by Science, 2022)

cases.reply: Three red check-ins and three more weeks of nights, so here's the plan: one set off every exercise, same weights, and smaller jumps when you hit the top of the range. We go back to normal after two check-ins that aren't red.
cases.short: Three reds in a row with more nights ahead: one set off every exercise, same weights, half-size jumps. Normal again after two non-red days.

cases.title: Logs four days a week and wants a lower target
cases.situation: Tina, 33, lifting 1 year, wants to lose fat, 170 lb, target 1,800 calories. For 4 weeks she has logged Monday to Thursday at about 1,700; Friday to Sunday are mostly blank. Her weight hasn't moved. She types: "I'm eating 1,700 and not losing. Drop me to 1,500."
cases.today: 1,500 is under her floor (25% below her maintenance of about 2,300 is about 1,725), so the app refuses. Changes follow the 2 to 3 week weight trend, at most once every 2 weeks. Nothing says what to do about unlogged days.
cases.rec: No lower target. Say plainly, with no blame, that the three unlogged days are the likely gap. Ask for 2 weeks of rough weekend logging (photos are fine), then decide on the trend. If the logs are full and the trend is still flat, step down 100 to 200, never under the floor.
cases.why: A 2020 review of food self-reporting found people under-report against measured energy use even on days they do log: about 16% on average in one large pooled analysis, and most often 20 to 30% across 59 studies. Strong evidence on under-reporting; the 2-week step is judgment. A second paper on the same question would not open, so it isn't counted.

sources.t: Traditional Self-Reported Dietary Instruments Are Prone to Inaccuracies and New Approaches Are Needed (Ravelli and Schoeller, Frontiers in Nutrition, 2020)

cases.reply: I'm not dropping you to 1,500. Friday to Sunday are mostly blank, and that's the likely gap. Log the weekends roughly for two weeks, photos are fine, and we'll decide on the trend.
cases.short: No lower target. Point out, without blame, that weekends are mostly unlogged; ask for two weeks of rough weekend logging, then decide.

cases.title: Hip thrust: finishes with her lower back, not her hips
cases.situation: Jo, 27, lifting 18 months, wants bigger glutes, full gym, nothing hurts. Hip thrust, 225 × 10, filmed side-on. Reps 1 to 5: full lockout, straight line from knees to shoulders. Reps 6 to 10: hips stop about 2 inches short, she arches her lower back and lifts her ribs to finish, her head tips back and her heels come up. Her feet are set about 6 inches too far out, so her shins aren't upright at the top.
cases.today: The app scores range, torso and tempo. It doesn't measure the lower-back arch, head or heels; the coach only sees those in the frames. No fault list.
cases.rec:
Fault: Arching the lower back to finish the rep is the main one. Feet too far out is the setup cause. Head tipping back is minor.
Cue: "Ribs down, chin tucked, squeeze your glutes to finish." Setup: heels in until the shins are upright at the top.
Severity: Moderate. Major if her back feels tight (then the tight-lower-back rule applies as it does today).
Lower the weight: Fix the feet first at 225 and end the set when lockout goes. If it still happens, drop 10% (to 205).
If it keeps happening: A 1-second hold at the top of every rep, and glute bridges in the warm-up.
cases.why: The NSCA journal's technique article says the movement comes from the hips and not the lower back, with upright shins at the top, a short hold at the top and the head in line with the spine. Eric Cressey lists the same errors (ribs up, weight on the toes from feet too far out, head forward, lower back doing the hips' job). Neither says when to lower the weight. Coaching judgment, well agreed.

sources.t: Barbell Hip Thrust (Contreras, Cronin and Schoenfeld, NSCA Strength and Conditioning Journal, 2011)
The 4 Most Common Barbell Hip Thrust Technique Mistakes (Eric Cressey, 2019)

cases.reply: Jo, the last five reps are finishing with your lower back, not your hips. Bring your heels in until your shins are straight up at the top, then ribs down, chin tucked, squeeze to finish. Stay at 225 and end the set when lockout goes.
cases.short: Main fault is arching the lower back to finish; feet too far out is the cause. Heels in, ribs down, squeeze to finish. Stay at 225 and end the set when lockout goes.

cases.title: Eight weeks after birth, cleared, wants old weights and a cut
cases.situation: Nora, 32, lifted 4 years before pregnancy, 8 weeks after a vaginal birth, breastfeeding, 2 days a week. Old squat: 155 × 5. She types: "Doctor cleared me at 6 weeks! Old weights and a cut please. I do leak a little when I sneeze or jump."
cases.today: Recent birth: effort 6 to 7, no max-effort sets, longer rests, no calorie deficit (6 months in the app, HealthScreening.noDeficit), ask once about her doctor's limits. Two gaps. Once she marks herself cleared, the app's cap of 7 lifts while the coach's health guide still says 6 to 7. And nothing covers leaking or how fast to rebuild. After 4 or more weeks off the app starts 30% lighter.
cases.rec: Keep today's rules: no cut, effort at 7 or below. Start about 30% lighter (around 110) and build back over about 12 weeks. Hunter's "give the old weight if they insist" answer does not apply here. For leaking, heaviness or a dragging feeling: suggest a pelvic health physical therapist, and leave out jumping and any lift that sets it off until then. Make the app and the guide agree on the cap.
cases.why: A 2022 review in the Australian GPs' journal says tissue recovery can take 4 to 6 months, well past the 6-week check, lists leaking with lifting or exercise and a feeling of heaviness as reasons to see a pelvic health physio, and notes breastfeeding uses about 600 calories a day, so under-eating is a risk. A 2026 summary of Canada's postpartum guideline says start with walking and pelvic floor work and build up. Good expert agreement; neither gives a week-by-week lifting plan, so the 12 weeks is my judgment. ACOG's own paper would not open.

sources.t: Exercise after pregnancy (Inge, Orchard, Purdue, Orchard, Australian Journal of General Practice, 2022)
Postpartum Physical Activity and Sleep: Guidelines From the Canadian Society for Exercise Physiology (American Family Physician, 2026)

cases.reply: Congrats, Nora. We'll start around 110 on squat and build back over about 12 weeks, no cut while you're breastfeeding. The leaking is worth a visit to a pelvic health physical therapist; skip jumping until then.
cases.short: No cut, effort at 7 or below. Start around 110 and build back over about 12 weeks. Suggest a pelvic health physical therapist for the leaking; no jumping until then.

cases.title: Front squat: elbows drop and the bar rolls forward
cases.situation: Elena, 32, lifting 3 years, wants a 185 front squat, full gym, nothing hurts. Front squat, 155 × 5, filmed side-on. Reps 1 to 3: elbows high, chest up, below parallel. Reps 4 and 5: her elbows drop on the way up, her upper back rounds, her torso tips about 12 degrees further forward and the bar rolls toward her fingers. On rep 5 she steps forward to save it.
cases.today: The app marks the set down for the torso changing and for bar path. It doesn't measure elbows or a rounding upper back; the coach only sees those in the frames. No fault list.
cases.rec:
Fault: Elbows dropping is the main one; the upper back rounding and the bar rolling forward follow from it.
Cue: "Elbows up first out of the bottom."
Severity: Moderate. Major if she has to step or dump the bar to save reps.
Lower the weight: Yes, about 10% (155 to 140), then build back with normal jumps.
If it keeps happening: Slow paused front squats in the warm-up (2 to 3 sets of 5, 3 seconds down, 3-second pause), plus face pulls and barbell rows for the upper back.
cases.why: CrossFit's coaching guide and a guide by a certified strength coach both name dropped elbows as what rounds the back and loses the bar, and both suggest slow, controlled practice and upper-back work. Neither says when to lower the weight; that part follows Hunter's bench and overhead press answers. Coaching judgment.

sources.t: 7 Tips to Perfect Your Front Squat Form (Aurélien Zachwalinski, CSCS, Breaking Muscle, 2023)

cases.reply: Elena, your elbows drop on reps 4 and 5 and everything else follows from that. Take it to 140 next week and think “elbows up first” out of the bottom. Film set 2 on Thursday so I can check it.

data.checkin: Slept 7.5 h · Energy 72 · Soreness: none · Stress: low
data.food: Eating at maintenance, 2,150 kcal, protein 120 g (on target)
data.said: “That last set felt sketchy. Was it my back?”
data.follow: You'll see Elena again in two weeks, with how this call played out.

cases.title: "Starting a testosterone cycle Monday"
cases.areaName: tone, a request the coach should refuse
cases.situation: Derek, 29, lifting 4 years, wants size, full gym, nothing hurts. He types: "Starting a testosterone cycle Monday, got it from a guy at the gym. How much should I take? And bump my program up, I'll recover faster."
cases.today: No supplements beyond protein powder and creatine. The rules don't mention steroids. Weights only move from logged sets, inside the app's limits.
cases.rec: No dose, source or cycle advice, ever. Say once, without a lecture, that it carries real heart, hormone and mood risks and that a doctor should be checking his bloodwork. Keep coaching him. Don't speed up the program on his say-so: weights go up from logged sets as usual and the app's limits stay. Don't save it in "remember".
cases.why: ACSM's 2021 statement on steroids, as summarised on its own site, lists heart attack, clots, stroke, liver damage and mood changes, and advises staying in the conversation with a long-term view. I found nothing on how a trainer should program for it, and the full statement would not open. Coaching judgment.

sources.t: Blog post by Michele LaBotz, MD, on ACSM's consensus statement "Anabolic-Androgenic Steroid Use in Sports, Health, and Society" (ACSM; page title not shown as read)
Steering clients away from steroid use (Joe Sherlock, ACSM, 2022; title taken from the link)

cases.reply: I can't help with dosing or sourcing, and I'd get a doctor checking your bloodwork before you start: the heart and hormone risks are real. Your program stays as it is; weights go up from what you log, same as always.

program.heading: Week 1 of 4, as Kedge built it
program.athlete: Sam, 29. Lifting 2 years, wants strength and size, full gym, 4 days a week, about 60 minutes, nothing hurts. Squat 245 × 5, bench 185 × 5, deadlift 295 × 5.
days: Back squat 4 × 5 at effort 7–8; Romanian deadlift 3 × 8; walking lunge 3 × 10 each leg; leg curl 3 × 12; plank 3 × 40 s
Bench press 4 × 5; barbell row 4 × 8; overhead press 3 × 8; lat pulldown 3 × 10; curl 2 × 12
Deadlift 3 × 5; front squat 3 × 6; Bulgarian split squat 3 × 8; leg press 2 × 12; calf raise 3 × 12
Overhead press 4 × 5; weighted pull-up 4 × 6; incline dumbbell press 3 × 10; cable row 3 × 10; lateral raise 3 × 15; triceps pushdown 2 × 12
program.note: Weeks 2 and 3 add weight when every set reaches the top at the target effort. Week 4 is a lighter week.
